strengths: Proposes a learned unmasking policy for masked diffusion models (MDMs), replacing heuristic schedules with a KL-regularized MDP optimized via GRPO. The approach is practical and memory-efficient: it freezes the large MDM and trains a small policy head, feasible on a single A100 40GB GPU.

Provides theoretical analysis, including a restatement of GRPO convergence, a KL-tightening theorem under assumptions, and tractable surrogate objectives (gradient alignment and KL surrogate) to connect theory to practical training.

Evaluates on four benchmarks (Sudoku, Zebra, GSM8K, MATH500) using LLaDA-8B, showing consistent improvements over random, margin, entropy, and max-confidence heuristics; the Sudoku gain (70.5% to 81.7%) is notable.
Includes ablations on reference-policy choices (max-confidence, softmax, Top-K) and compatibility with diffu-GRPO, demonstrating additional gains when combined with post-training of the base MDM.
The method is well-motivated: max-confidence is a strong but not optimal heuristic, and the paper empirically shows that higher-yield unmasking trajectories exist (Pass@N experiments).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: RL for learning unmasking policies in MDMs has already been explored by DColT (Huang et al., 2025). The main new ingredient is KL regularization with an explicit reference policy, which is a fairly direct adaptation of GRPO. No direct comparison to DColT in the main results; the 'random initialization' ablation is not equivalent to DColT, which jointly trains the MDM and policy.

Theoretical claims are overbroad. Theorem 2 requires a support condition and binary reward r=1 on the support of the ideal data distribution. This does not hold for the deterministic max-confidence reference (for which they instead use cross-entropy regularization) nor for logic-puzzle benchmarks where the reward is fractional. Thus the claim that the optimized policy is provably closer to the data distribution than heuristic schedules is not fully supported.

The practical loss (clipped GRPO, token-wise surrogate, Monte Carlo approximation) differs from the theoretical objective. Convergence and improvement guarantees do not directly apply to the implemented algorithm; the connection relies on approximations and additional assumptions.

Evaluation lacks error bars or significance tests for main results. Some improvements are small (e.g., Zebra 0.362 vs. 0.351 for entropy; MATH500 0.284 ties margin), so it is unclear whether gains are statistically meaningful. Only one base model (LLaDA-8B) is tested.

Missing important baselines: DColT (Huang et al., 2025) is the closest prior work that also learns an unmasking policy via RL, but it is not included in the main comparison tables. No comparison to other learned schedulers or larger-scale MDMs.

Reproducibility is limited: hyperparameters, training data splits, compute budget, and reward details are not fully specified. No code or model release is mentioned. There is also an inconsistency in reward definition (binary vs. fractional) across sections.

The regularization ablation is mixed: Figure 4 suggests that on Sudoku the CE regularizer may reduce group-reward standard deviation, contradicting the claim that it maintains larger variance. Only GSM8K shows the claimed higher standard deviation.
Clarity and formatting issues: typos (e.g., 'let let'), repeated equation numbers, garbled Table 1, and duplicated figure captions make some parts difficult to follow.

strengths: Targets a relevant and timely problem: the unmasking order in masked diffusion models strongly affects generation quality, and learning a scheduler beyond hand-designed heuristics is a sensible direction.
Formulates unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP with an explicit reference policy and adapts a GRPO-style objective, which gives an organized framework for policy optimization.
Proposes a memory-efficient implementation that keeps the base MDM frozen and trains only a small unmasking policy head, reportedly on a single A100 40GB GPU.
Reports gains on four benchmarks, with a substantial improvement on Sudoku and compatibility with diffu-GRPO, suggesting the learned policy can complement existing MDM post-training.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. RL-trained unmasking policies for masked diffusion models already exist (e.g., DCoLT/Huang et al. 2025), and the claimed KL-regularized MDP + reference-policy formulation is an incremental variation. Theorem 1 is essentially a restatement of Mroueh (2025), so it does not constitute a new theoretical contribution.

The theoretical guarantees are not convincingly established for the practical method. Theorem 2 relies on strong assumptions (ideal MDM θ*, support inclusion, and pθ* assigning probability only to correct answers) that are questionable and do not cover the deterministic g_conf used in experiments. The CE surrogate used for g_conf is outside the KL theorem, so the central theoretical claim is not properly connected to the main empirical setup.

The surrogate-loss results are local/approximate. Proposition 1 only gives approximate gradient equality under φ ≈ φ_old and exactness only at the first step, while the actual training uses clipping, Monte Carlo sampling, finite groups, and multiple updates. There is no rigorous error bound or convergence analysis for the implemented algorithm.

Evaluation is insufficient for a top-tier venue. Only one base MDM (LLaDA-8B) and four benchmarks are used; there is no main-table comparison to DCoLT or other learned schedulers. Several improvements are marginal (e.g., Zebra 0.362 vs. 0.351, MATH500 ties the best baseline), and statistical significance, seeds, and variance are not reported.

Reproducibility is lacking. The paper does not provide code, detailed hyperparameters, compute budget, prompt templates, reward implementation, training-set sizes, or variance across runs. The memory-efficient training algorithms are described, but key experimental details are still missing.

The title/abstract overclaim 'beyond explicit reference policies' while the method centrally depends on explicit reference policies and heuristic initializations. It learns relative to heuristics rather than removing them, so the framing is misleading.

Baselines and ablations are incomplete. The paper only compares against rule-based schedulers and does not ablate policy architecture, reference-policy choice, reward design, sequence length, bin size, or inference cost. There is also no wall-clock or compute trade-off analysis, which matters for claims of practical improvement.

Clarity and presentation need substantial work. Notation is dense and sometimes inconsistent, equation references are messy, and Table 1 is garbled/illegible in the provided manuscript. Claims such as 'consistently outperforms max-confidence' are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Introduces a principled KL-regularized MDP formulation for learning unmasking policies in masked diffusion models, going beyond fixed heuristics such as max-confidence.

Provides theoretical support: convergence/policy-improvement via GRPO dynamics and a KL-tightening result showing the learned terminal distribution can be closer to the ideal data distribution than the reference policy.

Derives practical surrogate objectives and several reference-policy realizations, including softmax, Top-K, and max-confidence variants, with a memory-efficient training algorithm that keeps the large MDM frozen.
Empirical results are promising: strong gains on Sudoku (81.7% vs. 70.5% for confidence) and consistent improvements on Zebra, GSM8K, and MATH500, including additional gains on top of diffu-GRPO.
Ablations and training-dynamics plots provide useful evidence that KL/CE regularization maintains exploration variance and improves convergence over random-initialized policy learning.
weaknesses: The closest prior learned unmasking-policy method, DColT (Huang et al., 2025), is not directly compared against; the 'random initialization' ablation is not equivalent to DColT because DColT can jointly train the base MDM, so the claim of superiority over learned policies is not fully substantiated.

Theoretical guarantees depend on restrictive assumptions, e.g., existence of an ideal zero-loss MDM and support containment of the ideal distribution by the reference policy. These assumptions may not hold for Top-K or deterministic max-confidence references, and the max-confidence realization uses CE rather than the theoretically justified KL surrogate.

Several empirical gains are modest (e.g., Zebra +0.011, MATH500 ties max-margin, GSM8K +0.019 over confidence), and the paper does not report confidence intervals or multiple seeds, leaving statistical significance and robustness unclear.

Training/evaluation protocols are not fully specified: it is unclear whether the policy is trained and evaluated on disjoint splits for each benchmark, how hyperparameters were selected, and whether code or sufficient reproducibility details will be released.

Presentation and notation contain issues: duplicated equation numbers, garbled Table 1 entries, typos ('let let'), and some appendix proofs/notation are difficult to verify, making the theoretical contributions harder to assess.

For GSM8K and MATH500, the Top-K reparameterization restricts exploration to the reference support, which limits the central claim that the method improves 'beyond' explicit reference policies in those settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in masked diffusion models: how to choose which position to unmask next during denoising.

Provides a principled formulation of unmasking as a KL-regularized MDP with a reference policy and a GRPO-style optimization objective, plus a memory-efficient implementation for training a small policy model against a frozen large MDM.
Includes theoretical results (convergence/fixed-point and KL-tightening claims) and derives tractable surrogate objectives.
Empirical results on Sudoku are strong, and there are additional ablations on regularization, dense vs. binary rewards, and compatibility with diffu-GRPO.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claim—that the learned policy provably yields samples closer to the data distribution than a strong heuristic—is not convincingly established. The proof relies on assumptions about the ideal MDM's support and reward structure that are not fully justified, and the key convergence theorem is largely a restatement of prior GRPO analysis rather than a new contribution.

The experiments do not directly compare against the reference policy used to train the method (e.g., Top-K) in the main tables. Since the method is explicitly designed to improve beyond a reference policy, this is a critical missing baseline. The choice of reference also varies per benchmark, raising concerns about per-benchmark tuning.

Empirical gains are uneven and often small: MATH500 ties the margin baseline, Zebra improvements are marginal, and GSM8K gains over max-confidence are modest. There are no error bars or significance tests, and best checkpoints are selected over training steps, which can inflate reported results.

Novelty is limited relative to prior work that also learns unmasking policies with RL (e.g., DColT). The paper distinguishes itself mainly through KL regularization and a reference policy, but the practical algorithmic novelty and accompanying guarantees are incremental.

The theoretical analysis assumes binary rewards, while the main experiments use dense or auxiliary rewards, including log-probability terms for math. This weakens the connection between the theory and the empirical validation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time unmasking order in masked diffusion models, where heuristics such as max-confidence are known to be strong but suboptimal.
Provides a clean KL-regularized MDP/GRPO formulation for learning an unmasking policy while keeping the base MDM frozen, with a memory-efficient training recipe exploiting frozen MDM features.
Includes experiments on four benchmarks and shows a large improvement on Sudoku, where unmasking order is especially important, plus modest gains on GSM8K and Zebra over some heuristic baselines.
The theoretical discussion connects the proposed objective to existing GRPO convergence and KL-tightening arguments under idealized assumptions, which is at least directionally relevant.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: training an unmasking policy with reinforcement learning is already explored by DCoLT; the KL-regularized GRPO variant and the theoretical results largely adapt existing results (e.g., Mroueh 2025 and standard policy-gradient/KL surrogate arguments) rather than introducing fundamentally new methodology.

Theory-practice mismatch: the main theoretical guarantees assume an ideal MDM and binary rewards, but the main experiments use dense rewards and task-specific training on incomplete MDMs. Therefore the formal claims do not directly support the empirical results.

Evaluation is insufficient: there is no comparison against the actual DCoLT method or other learned unmasking policies. Baselines are only heuristic schedulers, and no statistical significance or error bars are reported.

Result strength is uneven: the learned policy only ties the best baseline on MATH500, gives marginal gains on Zebra, and modest gains on GSM8K; the large gain is mainly on Sudoku, suggesting task-specific overfitting rather than a general-purpose solution.
The method trains a separate unmasking policy per benchmark, with no evidence of generalization across tasks or domains. This limits practical significance and scalability.
Methodological concern: the paper reports the best test-set checkpoint rather than a fixed final checkpoint, which can inflate reported accuracy and complicate reproducibility.
Reproducibility issues: the code link appears incomplete, and compute costs, training details, and reward design are not sufficiently reported for full replication.

Overstated claims: the abstract says the learned policy consistently outperforms max-confidence, but max-confidence is not always the strongest baseline, and the improvements are often small or tied with other heuristics.

Ablation and baseline fairness: random initialization is described as conceptually equivalent to DCoLT, which is not a faithful DCoLT baseline; there is no comparison against DCoLT-trained policies or other RL objectives under matched settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in masked diffusion models: choosing which position to unmask next.
Provides a principled RL formulation with a KL-regularized MDP and theoretical analysis of policy improvement and KL tightening.
Proposes a memory-efficient training scheme that freezes the base MDM and trains a lightweight unmasking policy, making the approach practical for large models.
Reports meaningful gains on Sudoku and improvements over max-confidence across four benchmarks (Sudoku, Zebra, GSM8K, MATH500).
Includes useful ablations on regularization and compatibility with diffu-GRPO, showing the learned scheduler can be combined with post-training methods.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited relative to prior RL-based unmasking-policy work such as DColT; the theoretical results largely restate/adapt existing GRPO convergence analysis rather than introducing fundamentally new theory.

The theoretical guarantees do not directly support the strongest empirical configuration: SUDOKU/ZEBRA use max-confidence CE regularization rather than the KL-regularized objective, and main experiments use dense/auxiliary rewards while Theorem 2 assumes binary rewards.
Missing direct comparison to the closest RL-based unmasking-policy baseline (DColT) in the final result tables; only informal training-curve comparisons are provided.

Evaluation protocol is concerning: the paper reports best accuracy over checkpoints on test benchmarks, lacks multiple seeds/confidence intervals, uses only one base MDM, and selects the reference policy per benchmark, which can lead to optimistic or overfit results.

The practical KL surrogate is not fully justified: Proposition 2 only shows trajectory-wise KL upper-bounds output-level KL, and decreasing an upper bound does not guarantee monotonic decrease of the output-level KL.

There is a theory-practice gap: Proposition 1 provides only approximate gradient alignment, and output-level GRPO convergence does not directly apply to the token-wise surrogate objective actually optimized.
Reproducibility is weakened by the blank code URL and incomplete details for baseline implementations and reward shaping.
Generalizability is not well established: gains on GSM8K and MATH500 are modest, MATH500 ties the margin baseline, and no results are shown on other MDMs or broader natural-language tasks.
